1.	Has the government any specific program to relieve unemployment this winter? If so, what is that program?
2.	Has the winter employment committee in Ottawa any executive powers to pursue an employment program on behalf of the government?
3.	What are the terms of reference of this committee and how does it operate?
4.	Are any cabinet ministers members of the committee? If so, which ones?

The answer to part 1 is as follows. There is a specific program the object of which is to increase winter employment so as to alleviate the normal seasonal slump in Canada. The program, known as the winter employment campaign or program, aims at providing an industrial and occupational climate favourable to the planning and execution of projects in the wintertime where possible.
The program, which is being jointly administered by the Department of Labour and the national employment service, enlists the services of national and local organizations, municipal groups and all available publicity media to make employers winter employment conscious. It enlists the support of federal government departments in undertaking new construction, maintenance, repairs and renovations in winter as well as procurement of supplies, where at all practicable. It sponsors a nation-wide information and publicity program.
Through winter employment committees across Canada, working closely with local employment offices, the program is co-ordinated on a nation-wide basis. Successful prosecution of the program is made possible through co-operation by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Labour Congress, the Canadian Construction Association, the Canadian Retail Federation, the Canadian Bankers' Association, the Canadian and Catholic Confederation of Labour and a number of other public-spirited groups who have lent their willing assistance. Provincial and municipal governments are also cooperating splendidly in scheduling projects in wintertime.
The answer to part 2 is as follows. The interdepartmental committee on winter employment is made up of representatives of a number of departments. Its special interest is in scheduling, where possible and practicable, federal works in wintertime. Its powers are purely advisory.
The answer to part 3 is as follows. This is a committee established to advise cabinet on federal government participation on a departmental level in the winter employment program.
The committee endeavours to obtain information on projects which might suitably be carried on in winter and makes recommendations accordingly. It also attempts to co-ordinate these various efforts on an interdepartmental basis.
The answer to question 4 is no.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Postmaster General, of which notice has been given. Can the minister say as to whether the removal of railway mail cars from the 300-mile run from Saskatoon to Edmonton will not result in poorer mail service to the citizens in that area; and does the minister intend to remove other railway mail cars in other sections of the country in an economy attempt, without regard to service?

subtopic: SASKATOON-EDMONTON    EFFECT OF REMOVAL OF RAILWAY MAIL CARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the action referred to was dictated because it was felt that the revised arrangement would result in an improved mail service, and it originated from complaints and information we received from that area that certain connections were not satisfactory.
To deal with the second and more general part of the question, I would say that the Post Office Department has never removed railway mail car service in an economy attempt without regard to service, and there certainly is not any intention of doing so in the future. Where railway mail cars have been removed and replaced by highway service it was for the purpose of improving the mail service, and in many cases because it was the only course of action to follow, the railways having removed the trains or changed them so that no adequate equipment was available. The economy factors which enter into this question are sizeable at times, but they are not the main consideration.

Mr. Chairman, it is not unusual for a man to inquire into the budget of a woman at home, but I think you will agree it is a distinction for a member of parliament to be the first to speak on the estimates of the hon. lady who sits as a minister of the crown. I think all members of this house will join me in congratulating the minister on the presentation of her first estimates.
(Translation):
I congratulate you, Madam, upon your appointment as Secretary of State and hope

that you will put all your abilities as a hardworking and genial lady at the service of your department.
(Text) :
The Department of the Secretary of State, Mr. Chairman, is not too well known to the public at large, but it is an important department dealing with a variety of matters of vital interest to the administration of our country. I do believe that more time should be devoted to the discussion of the estimates of this department, and that the members of this house should know more about the functions of its several branches. I am sure that during another session the minister will welcome a more detailed inquiry.
One of the functions of the Secretary of State is to report on the civil service commission. I am always happy to hear hon. members refer to the devotion, loyalty and standard of efficiency of our civil service. I thoroughly agree, and I believe this is at least one legacy whose transfer to the new government will stand them in good stead. What the civil service requires most, Mr. Chairman, is security and fair and honest treatment in matters of wages and promotion.
I have always said that we have the finest civil service in the world, but that we should also be the model employers. There are very important matters which confront the Secretary of State and the civil service commission, and I believe the time has come when the Civil Service Act should be revised to define and enlarge, if necessary, the powers of the commission; to establish its authority in certain matters relating to employee selection, salaries and promotion.
There has always been an open space between the treasury board and the civil service commission which allows for a great deal of ball-throwing and delay to the disadvantage of the civil service. In recent days we have heard rumours that a royal commission may be named to inquire into this matter. The minister might tell us if that subject has been discussed or whether it is the government's feeling that this is the proper course to follow. On the other hand, there has been talk that the commission itself is working on amendments to the Civil Service Act. Is it the intention to present any such amendments at this or future sessions? I am of the opinion that it would be much better if the government suggested its own revision of the Civil Service Act and gave the members of this house an opportunity to inquire into the matter. I do not think we should leave to others this task, which is essentially one belonging to the government and the House of Commons.
I might inquire also, Mr. Chairman, whether or not the minister has had any
Supply-Secretary of State recent talks with the civil service associations in connection with collective bargaining and strike rights. There was much publicity about this some time ago. I believe that much has to be done to clarify the situation in the minds of civil servants and the public at large, but our first endeavour in any event must be to preserve for the civil servants of Canada conditions of employment which are the most favourable anywhere.
I should like to be brief, Mr. Chairman, and I do not want to deal with all the branches of the minister's department, but rather than stand up repeatedly I would direct inquiries to a few subjects at this time.
Has the minister received any of the reports of the royal commission on patents, trade-marks and copyrights? If the answer is in the affirmative, when were they received and when does she propose to table them? I do not need to ask the minister about whether the patent office will be moved this year to the experimental farm. I think it is a bad move initiated under the former government, but I had great hopes that the new administration would have seen eye to eye with me, the public and interested parties.
Finally, and to be brief, I would appreciate it if the minister would tell us whether all salary adjustments have been completed in the printing bureau. I am particularly interested in the case of the pressmen.
I think the minister will agree that I have been short. She may expect that on other occasions I will have something further to say. However, I wish to repeat what I said at the beginning, namely that this department is one which I hope will be given a little bit more publicity because extremely important branches of government fall under it.

speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman. If we are on the first item I want to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Ottawa East in extending my sincere congratulations to the hon. member for having been the first lady in this country appointed to the cabinet. Knowing her as an opposition member and finding out what a genial person she is I am sure the opposition members of this house will get along with her just as cordially now that she is in a position of much greater responsibility.
I am wondering whether she can give us any further information-I think the question has already been asked-as to when the various reports of the royal commission on

patents, trade-marks, copyrights and so on will be tabled and made available to the members. I know that the commission [DOT] vas set up in the summer of 1954, and that apparently the report it is to make on patents will be considerably delayed. Apparently they are just starting new hearings once again. I am wondering if there is some way in which the new administration can speed up the extremely important study which the royal commission is making in this field so that we may have the benefit of the recommendations of the royal commission to the end that the injustices in relation to patents may be corrected at an early date.
I believe that this is one of the most important studies that have been made in the country over the years. There has been a great deal of interest in the whole question of patents. There is a growing feeling that current patent law is not in the best interests of the nation, and that corporations are able, by way of patent registry, to prevent competition and to prevent developments and so in an extremely serious manner retard industrial growth, expansion and innovation in this country.
I might say that already in the past a number of eminent persons have appeared before the royal commission and some of them have been sponsored by two daily newspapers from Saskatchewan. I refer to the Regina Leader-Post and the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix. Both papers have taken a great interest in this field. I believe they have rendered an important public service. From my study of their submissions to the commission I express the hope that a substantial number of the propositions they have put forward may be in the report of the royal commission and its recommendations. Even more than I did a year ago when I made a statement on this subject, I believe there is no room for restrictive practices to prevent competition and to prevent industrial growth in this country.
Having regard to our development the matter is more serious today than it was even a year ago because we know that today we are losing the race with the soviet union in a great many industrial fields. We hear that statement from experts almost daily. Now that this new administration and this new parliament are declaring war on restrictive patents and restrictive practices that have grown up around the use of patents as a method of preventing -competition, I hope that the new government may be able to get action in this field at a much quicker pace than was the former administration. I would ask the minister, if she will, to make a general comment on this particular subject

and problem and to say whether she can hold out the hope that at an early date the report will be received from the royal commission on the question of patents. I would also ask whether she can say that any particular study is being made in that field by the present government in the hope that the recommended action may be taken.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
would like to appeal to the hon. minister, after congratulating her on her new position, with respect to a case which I think does involve a grave injustice. I believe the hon. lady's department covers the field of custodian of alien property. Under the Japanese peace treaty such property as may be seized under that treaty is retained by the custodian.
Supply-Secretary of State
I am referring to a case which I do not think has anything to do with war reparations but does involve a point of great personal injustice. In British Columbia two Canadians of Japanese origin, Mr. and Mrs. Kubodera, lived and became Canadian citizens; the husband was naturalized. In 1924 as they had no children of their own they adopted a Japanese girl; she lived with them for 12 years. In 1936 she returned to Japan where she became a music teacher and where she still lives and teaches music.
Mr. and Mrs. Kubodero are now dead, but they expressed in their valid last will and testament a desire that their estate should pass to the girl who was considered at the time of their death to be their adopted daughter. That estate was not large; the amount presently involved is, I believe, $6,325 but under our treaty with Japan, article 14, Canada specified that it shall retain, seize and liquidate the assets of any Japanese national. Under that provision the government of Canada is holding, and perhaps has already disposed into consolidated revenue, this sum of $6,325, which in their last wishes these two people wanted to pass on to their adopted daughter.
Now I think it is reasonable to say that when the Japanese peace treaty was concluded nothing of this sort was contemplated; I do not think we wanted to seize a relatively small estate such as has been left to this girl as part of war reparations which we could not otherwise exact from Japan. She, of course, is a private individual and it can hardly be suggested that she was to blame for the war.
While we run into situations in wars of this modern age where we cannot collect reparations from a whole people, it does not seem reasonable that we should turn about, as in this case, and seize a very small estate and chalk it up as some gain we have made in the way of collecting reparations from Japan.
Therefore, I hope the minister will look into this matter and see whether, in the interests of good relations with Japan which is a very good customer of Canada and a very important nation in Asia, it is worth while to hold on to this small estate left to a girl now living in Japan.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to associate myself with the remarks which have been made with respect to the hon. lady's elevation to the office she now holds. I would certainly be one of the first to congratulate her upon such a wonderful achievement and I am very much in agreement with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate in that it is certain as time goes on, should the government be in office, I am very sure she will

Supply-Secretary of State probably receive a portfolio of greater significance than the one she holds at present. Not that this one is unimportant. 1 do feel it is a very important portfolio since it has control over the civil service commission which is an essential part of our society. I have always made it a practice to devote a certain amount of time to discussing these particular estimates. I intend to do so again today.
With respect to the expenditures hon. members, particularly those who were here during the last parliament, will recognize they seem to increase. I have particular reference to the items for paper work. Here I notice there is quite a steep increase with respect to publications of departmental reports and other material, to which I have no doubt we will come later, but we have an increase of from $472,000 to $658,000 which is better than one-half of the total increase which the department requires for the operation of the office of Secretary of State.
This figure is a most important one and I was just wondering, when I viewed the overall chart which indicated the comparison between last year's estimates and this year's estimates, why there should be such a marked difference in this particular field as compared with the others. I notice the other increase comes under civil service which accounts for approximately the balance of the change, a matter of $140,000 under civil service salaries and wages, making a total difference of about $320,000 or so in the actual estimates.
Now it does seem to me that this matter of the use of paper and stationery is a most important one in the operation of our governmental departments. I have frequently wondered, when I come on occasion to the House of Commons very early in the morning and find a heaping cartful of newspapers, exactly what does become of the paper. Is it used for some particular purpose? Does the government realize anything on the sale of it; is it consigned to an incinerator and burned or just what does become of the paper from this building alone, much less the Department of the Secretary of State? I would hope that the hon. lady in replying later would have something to say on this question and if the time permits and I should be in the house I will probably have more to say on the civil service and the operations of that part of the department. More particularly I would like information on this question having to do with paper.
Another question that has given me considerable concern is the Canada Elections Act and the part having to do with the operation of our elections. I will have certain recommendations and suggestions to make with respect to that at a later time, some of

which might cost us a little more money but all of which I hope will result in a little more efficiency in getting our electoral lists more completely arranged so we do not have so many names that should be on the voters list omitted by mistake. However, I will reserve my remarks in that respect for a later time.

Dealing now with the questions which were asked by the hon. member for Ottawa East. He first of all made some inquiries with regard to the civil service commission. I quite agree with him that the government of Canada should be the model employer. However, with reference to the establishment of a royal commission no such thought has entered the mind of the government to date but the civil service commission itself is considering all aspects of the relationship
Supply-Secretary of State of the employer to the employee in all departments where it is concerned. If it is found necessary to amend the act to bring about a better relationship I can assure the hon. member this government will be glad to welcome suggestions which are made to it in that respect.
The hon. member for Ottawa East also asked what progress had been made with regard to the institution of collective bargaining. I might say he knows as much about it as I do because I think everything that has happened to date has been reported in the newspapers and even some of the things that have not happened to date have already appeared in the newspapers. In making that last remark I have reference in particular to a much publicized meeting which was prophesied by the press and which has not yet taken place but which will take place in the near future.
With reference to the royal commission on patents, a matter which was brought up both by the hon. member for Ottawa East and the hon. member for Assiniboia, I would point out that on October 28 I answered a question which the hon. member for Assiniboia put to me with reference to the availability of these reports. At that time I told him that the report on copyrights was ready in English but a final draft in French was still in the process of being prepared. That is still the situation. I expect to have it shortly but in the meantime it has not come to hand. The hon. member for Ottawa East asked me when it would be tabled. I can assure him that it will be tabled just as soon as it is available.
Since I am speaking of the royal commission, I might refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia. I agree with him that there is every urgency in the matter of these reports. The commission was given a tremendous task and it must be borne in mind that the members of the commission have other duties as well as those imposed upon them by reason of this particular commission.
While it is true that the sittings on patents will be resumed in March, and it may seem to the hon. member that that is quite a long way off and that the report will be delayed by reason thereof, I should like to point out that we expect to have the report on industrial designs shortly. It is thought well to take this step by step and table the reports as they are ready rather than hold up all of the reports until such time as the complete result of the deliberations has been printed. I shall be very glad to inquire whether there is any way in which this work can be speeded up.

Supply-Secretary of State
Since he asked me to comment on the necessity for an early report, I might say I agree with him that it is in the interests of industrial growth that the matter of patents should be examined carefully; that the recommendations of the commission should be in the hands of the government with a view to taking such steps as may be feasible and desirable to protect our industrial life and the works of our inventors.
The hon. member for Ottawa East spoke about the move of the patent office and practically answered himself. This move was undertaken before this government came into power. In fact the plans were so far advanced that there was very little that could be done about it. Accordingly the move is proceeding or plans for the move are proceeding. Of course there are different opinions amongst those who are required to use the patent office and I can only say I hope that they will find they will be much better accommodated in their new quarters.
The hon. member's question with regard to the printing bureau perhaps could be answered by saying that some time ago I received a request for a conference with those concerned on the matter of salaries and wages. Probably the hon. member for Ottawa East had specific reference to what is now known as a time lag in the adoption of rates after negotiations by printing employees in other centres. I immediately answered the letter and said I would be very pleased to see those representatives at an early date and, to my surprise, they said they were not ready. Maybe they were not used to getting such a fast reply but in any event they were not ready and I am now waiting until such time as they are prepared to meet with me.
I assure the hon. member that I too would hope that bilingualism would grow in the civil service. Of course he understands as well as any that there are many parts of Canada where it is not necessary and where, even if it were a requirement of the service that a person should be bilingual, by reason of having no place in which to practice the second language it would soon fall into disuse. I know that from personal experience. It is unfortunate that the acquisition of a second language does not always bring with it the opportunity for its use. I could wish it were true in my own case.

I might say to him that, regardless of the sympathy which each and every one of us has for individual persons, this is a principle which has been adopted by all countries. It is not Canada alone which has adopted this principle, and even if we wanted to it would be almost impossible to differentiate between claimants. What is right for

one claimant is right for another without regard to the amount involved. It is unfortunate that as a result of wars many innocent people suffer not only financially but also in health and in other ways. The Queen's Printer, I may say, also has the authority to question what he considers to be any abnormal requisitions and sometimes he does just that. If so, I regret raising the matter again, but it is of importance and I would like a comment from the minister. In Vancouver I was informed during the last general election- and I am sure this is the case in respect to many other members in British Columbia -time after time that it was becoming almost impossible for union shops to compete and do the work in the preparation of the voters' lists and other material required in an election by the federal government because there had not been a change in the price that could be paid for such work.
Now in view of the statements made by the minister as recently as a few moments ago, I hope she is now in a position-bearing in mind that she is one who has in the past spoken so strongly in favour of the trade union movement-to give us an indication that, prior to the next election, the necessary
1346	HOUSE OF
Supply-Secretary of State changes will be made so that the union shops may be able to do the work required in the printing trades in a general election.
One other most important point, I think, to a great many if not all of the members of this house and to all candidates in all parties, is the assurance that those who are entitled to vote will know exactly where to vote. Under the present policy-indeed it may be the law-with respect to federal elections, after the lists of enumeration are closed the returning officer sends around a tear sheet upon which the voter's name appears. Now the fact that that tear sheet is sent to every person whose name is going to appear on the voters' list must be a mighty expensive proposition. This is a notification to the majority of the people that their names are on the list but it has been my very definite experience-and I think it must have been the experience of others-that most people upon receiving this tear sheet of the voters' list see their names thereon, feel happy and then the tear sheet goes into the wastepaper basket or the furnace. They do not notice that on the upper right hand corner of the tear sheet it tells them in very small print, that they vote at this or an approximate address. I do not know what has been the experience of the hon. minister but I do know the experience in my own constituency is that the phones are busy all day long with inquiries as to where to vote. We ask if they have not received a notification that they were on the voters' lists and they say "Yes". Then we ask "Did you not notice in the upper right hand corner it tells you where to vote?" The answer is no.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that in an act of parliament making provision for an election every care should be taken to ensure that the person knows where he votes. I can only speak provincially so far as British Columbia is concerned, but under our British Columbia provincial elections act no tear sheet is sent out at all. The returning officer sends to all those whose names are on the voters' list a post card telling them where they should vote. Now every person on receipt of that card knows he is on the voters' list and also knows exactly where to vote.
I would hope that it might be possible for something of that nature to be followed through on a federal basis but if it cannot be done immediately without a change in the act then I would suggest to the minister, through you, Mr. Chairman, that a change be made-and surely this does not require any amendment to the act-on the notification on the tear sheet in print of such size that the voter receiving this notification will know that this is the information as to where he


votes and will hang onto it. This action cannot be taken by the returning officer because I took it up with the returning officer in Vancouver East and he told me he had exactly the same thought. He tried to have the size of print increased in order that it would be brought to the attention of the recipient and he was told he could not change the size of the print. I am certain the minister wants everyone to know just where he should vote and I would ask if she could arrange to have the chief electoral officer give authority to the returning officers to put the notification as to where a person votes in larger print than it has ever appeared in the past. I see no reason why this cannot be done.
There are many other things that could be spoken about on the subject of the Canada Elections Act but I will rest content with these three matters I raised hoping that something will be done in the near future.

subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact the question of advance polls has been raised I would like to offer a suggestion to the minister which I am sure has been brought to her attention previously and that is the suggestion which has been raised by the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities for the last four years that some uniformity be attempted in the regulations as far as continuity of advance polls is concerned. I am not suggesting the act should be changed in order to satisfy municipal or provincial representations but they have presented very comprehensive briefs on the question of continuity and also on the question of flexibility which several hon. members have raised, both of which suggestions are valid.
Having experience in the province from which I come where such uniformity has now been reached it might well be that the minister will take this into consideration in view of the remarks that have been made because of course there has been confusion with regard to advance polls which has created a problem in the past.
Before resuming my seat I would point out that my name being what it is I certainly have no objection to the name Smith being kept on the sample ballot.

subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I know we have progressed far into the estimates of the Department of the Secretary of State but I would just like to add my words of congratulation to those that have been extended to the hon. lady on her elevation to the office of Secretary of State. I was impressed with the evident change in tone which has characterized the statements of various members as they have asked questions and made their contributions in this debate and it occurred

to me that if we ever reached the point where a lady headed up each and every department of government this house would be a very quiet place.

subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: It would be all lady members.

subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Many of the caustic comments would be omitted from our discussion and in fact it might even get monotonous at times.
We are now considering the estimates relating to the office of the chief electoral officer and several of the points I had intended to raise have already been raised by other hon. members, for instance the question of advance poll. I believe that the purpose should be to try and make it feasible for as many as possible of our citizens to vote in the various elections. If it requires changes in the act or in the regulations those changes should be effected because, as I have said, I believe that every qualified voter in the country should have the opportunity, shall I say with the least possible inconvenience, to cast his or her ballot in the elections that are held. I understand there are just certain areas designated under the Canada Elections Act where advance polls can be set up. There are also very close lines drawn as to who can vote at advance polls. I would suggest that consideration be given, not only to increasing the number of advance polls and placing them strategically across the country but also to extending the categories of those qualified to vote at advance polls.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: Why should there be any restrictions?

subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
I am being modest in my request. There are several other matters I would like to mention and one is the system of enumerating as it is now conducted. I have not any plan to offer in this particular respect but I believe the system of enumerating could be vastly improved in many areas. For instance, in the last election we found there were whole blocks of residences entirely left, out. I think I am safe in saying we found there were hundreds of eligible voters whose names did not appear on the lists at all. This may have been due to errors in human judgment but there were also instances where the names were given to the enumerators and then when a check was made at the time of the sitting of the court of revision the names were still not on the list and in some instances when those very same individuals went to vote on election day they found their names were still left off the list. I do not know just what can be done, whether it is a matter of enforcing the regulations or what other means can be employed to correct the situation, but I believe some attention should be given to these seeming irregularities in the matter of enumerating.
Supply-Secretary of State
Another problem is the posting of voters lists. This question was raised during the last campaign when we discovered that some of the voters lists were nailed up on trees in different places and many were defaced possibly by children or by the weather. The lists had become almost impossible to read and in some cases they had disappeared altogether. It was suggested that when this particular section governing the posting of voters lists was placed in the act it had reference to the days when there was a common meeting place in each community perhaps under some great tree and the lists were placed there in what was possibly the most convenient place to find them. I would suggest that the voters lists be posted somewhere where they will be protected from the elements and where some supervision could be given regarding the condition in which they are kept.
The court of revision should be set up in perhaps the most populated area of a community. As it is now, I believe that those who are responsible for the court of revision can set up the office possibly in their homes, but in some instances that home may be two miles from the most thickly populated area of that community or of that section. Therefore the people from the populated area have to make a journey of one or two miles and perhaps turn off to a side road somewhere and look around in the dark to find the place where they are to check their names. I suggest that some attention be given to this particular matter as well.
Then, there is the matter of the political affiliations of the candidates on the ballots. I know this has been turned down. It was turned down by the previous administration on the basis that we were elected as individuals and not as members of parties. I think we ought to be at least realistic. I know we can possibly look back and say, yes, that was so; but after all we have to keep up with the times in some respects. It would save a lot of confusion if the political affiliation of the candidate were included on the ballot. This would be of tremendous importance in the event of two, or perhaps even three, candidates having the same name and in some instances the same initials as well.
Therefore I make these suggestions and recommend that consideration be given to some of these matters with a view to eliminating some of these irregularities and in other respects bringing our election act more in line with present day realities.

subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
I also would like to congratulate the minister. I was afraid for some time last year that the first lady cabinet minister of the government was going to come from

Supply-Secretary of State my riding. I am quite pleased to congratulate the present incumbent.
I would like to mention the matter of printing. Over the years we have seen where the printing for elections has been done, and where a vast quantity is given out at one time, the system of patronage is quite often applied. This means that while there are a number of printing shops in an area which could do this kind of printing, because a particular printing company is a friend of the party that has the giving of this patronage the contracts for printing are sometimes done on that basis. In a number of instances it works a great deal of hardship. I can recall one printing shop that did the printing for three ridings, and the time limit had been reached before the printing was available. On a number of occasions the time had expired before the printing was done. The problem was raised in my riding in the last election. I think the printing could be spread around not only because I do not believe in the principle of patronage in this matter or in anything else but because it would facilitate getting the printing done a lot sooner and would meet the requirements of the time limit.
I have another matter I should like to discuss, namely the voting of service personnel. I had the unfortunate privilege this year of being able to see all the ballots of the service personnel in my particular riding. I do not expect that to happen again, but it did give us the opportunity of seeing some of the things that were wrong with the system that we are now using in service personnel voting.
There is a time in December when the service personnel name the riding from which they come. When that is done I think lists should be made available to the candidates on the same basis as the voters' lists from municipalities are made available. We find that it is almost impossible for a candidate to find out not only the areas that the service personnel are in but also how many service personnel are in a particular riding. In most instances we do not come within 100 per cent of guessing how many service personnel there may be in a particular riding.
In discussions with some of the service personnel we find that there are a lot of things to be desired in the methods they use for taking the votes of the service personnel. We are told that-obviously the ballots that I saw and the areas from which they come bear this out-some particular areas are well represented. A large vote comes from them. Other areas have no votes coming from them. A directive should be issued to the officers in charge of voting along

with information for election purposes and all the service personnel should be given the same kind of information as to who are their candidates and the ridings in which they are registered, together with all other pertinent information.
In a provincial election I had the opportunity to visit one of our large army camps at election time. In that particular camp the commanding officer informed me that he had no interest whatsoever in elections; he was not going to get mixed up in them, and no election discussion would take place at his particular camp. He would have been quite happy if they had declared all the service personnel out of bounds. The result is that one particular party who has a friend in that camp reaps the advantage. There will be a large vote.
We have examined the vote in this particular instance. The information which was given was in most instances one-sided. At the end of the year, in December, when the list is compiled-and I understand it can be changed only once a year-they should be made available. If the particular lists, with the number of people and the names of the people, can be made available, as is done in municipal elections, and still meet security requirements then that should be done.
Perhaps I should tell the committee why I saw the ballots in the last federal election. There was a recount and obviously we had the opportunity to examine them and find out from what areas they came.
There is another problem that enters into the situation when there is an army camp in a certain area. The service personnel themselves are listed as being registered in whatever district or riding they choose. As I said, they make their choice at the end of the year. But if they have their wives with them at the camp, then the wives must vote in the riding in which the camp is located. That in turn works another hardship because, if there is no method-and I think there obviously should be some method-of getting information to those people who are voting in that riding-in this instance the wives of the service personnel-hon. members can see the difficulties which arise.
In a recent election I was informed in Camp Borden that there were going to be no public meetings; no posters were to be allowed and there was going to be no literature distributed, although at that time there were 700 women in the riding who were eligible to vote. Therefore, I think some consideration should be given to changing the act. If we believe-and I think we all do-that our service personnel have the right to vote, then I think they have the right to know who they are to vote for. They should

be given some information and that should not be just the prerogative of certain candidates. All candidates should be entitled to that information, and I think the women who are in the riding should be treated as other citizens in that riding, and they should be allowed to hold public meetings, or whatever the candidates decide amongst themselves should be done.

subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
I should like to add to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Fraser Valley with regard to the posting of voters' lists. He brought to the attention of the committee that these lists are exposed to the weather and are subject to being torn up by children or damaged in other ways with the result that they may not be complete. When the tear sheet is sent out people are notified that they are already on the list but there are always some people who are missed. To overcome that I suggest that there should be some central place in each subdivision where the lists can be seen. The location should be advertised and, if necessary, certain hours in the day should be set and someone should be there to give further information if it is needed.
I think it is a very necessary part of the enumeration process that the lists be posted and what I have suggested will overcome many of the difficulties that have been encountered during an election. It is a simple thing. It would only cost a little extra. These lists are exposed to the weather and subject to the hazard of being pulled off the post. The only way we can overcome that is to have the lists available under cover at some central spot.

subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while I am sure the majority of members recognize that we can improve the election act by a number of amendments, I am also sure that for two reasons we can be proud of the way in which elections are conducted generally in Canada. The first is the sense of fair play that exists among the Canadian people. The second is the excellent and efficient senior officers who administer the act.
In view of the thousands who are denied the opportunity to vote under the present act, I support wholeheartedly the representations made by previous speakers regarding certain amendments, particularly with respect to an extension of the qualifications in the case of those who are entitled to vote at advance polls. My constituency is one of those that are particularly affected by the restrictions in the present act. We have large numbers of lumbermen and miners who have to work some distance away from home.
It is the practice in large sections of my constituency for loggers and lumbermen to travel anywhere from 20 to 50 miles to work 96698-86i
Supply-Secretary of State and to return during the week ends, often by water transportation, sometimes by air or over rough mountain roads. Quite frequently a man returns for the week end or for a few days to the village in which he resides and then has to leave on Sunday to be back at work for Monday morning. Because it is not possible for these lumbermen and loggers to return at any reasonable expense for election day they are denied their right to vote under the present act. The same situation applies to a lesser number of miners in my constituency, particularly those who are working in small mines at high levels and in isolated places.
But we have a particular situation in the interior of British Columbia that I want to bring to the minister's attention, and I presume it exists in other forested portions of Canada. Large numbers of men can be denied the opportunity to vote on election day should they be called away to fight a forest fire. To illustrate, Mr. Chairman, some three or four days before the last election on June 10 a large fire started in the Big Bend country of the Columbia river.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: Who started it?

subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
I think it was started by lightning at high levels. In order to meet such a fire menace in very large and valuable stands of timber it is often necessary to mobilize several hundred men and get them to the scene of the fire as soon as possible. In our district it is nothing unusual for all the mills to be closed down and anywhere from 100 to 300 men quickly mobilized and transported 100 or 125 miles. This fire was 175 miles away from the home towns and villages of the men who were gathered together to fight it. Here they were taken away on Thursday or Friday without the opportunity to vote at advance polls.
They were faced with this question. These men value their votes. These are men who should have the right to vote like all other Canadians should. Under the law they would have been able to leave the scene of the fire but it would take so long that if they demanded their right under the act to have the opportunity to vote they would have only been able to work about half a day and then return to their home towns in order to vote. Fire is a very serious thing in our district because the economy depends to a great extent on the forest industry, the sawmills and so on. These men decided to go to the fire. The heads of several lumber companies concerned telephoned me and also telephoned the returning officer but I said that the law was the law and we could not get around it under these circumstances. I

Supply-Secretary of State did promise to bring the matter to the attention of the house at the first opportunity.
A large number of men were mobilized to fight this fire and they proceeded to the Big Bend country in the upper reaches of the Columbia. Happily the weather turned mild and there was some rain at high levels. By working like the very devil indeed they were able to put the fire out by Saturday night and they arrived back at their home villages in time to vote on Monday, fortunately for me.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: And for them.

subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
And for them, I trust. Anyway, Mr. Chairman, I bring this matter to the attention of the minister because this situation can develop very quickly anywhere that forest fires are likely to occur in British Columbia, and I think other members will corroborate me in that respect. The result is that hundreds of men can be disfranchised under such a situation.
I urge two things upon the minister. I urge that very serious consideration be given by the minister to the extension of the qualifications for those with the right to vote at advance polls in view of the numbers denied the right at the present time who are working in the lumbering and mining industries and the relatively large numbers who can be denied the opportunity to vote in forested country should we be faced with a serious fire situation.
Second, I do think that to meet this situation fully and properly there should be an increase in the number of advance polls. At the present time it is usual to have advance polls in some of the larger centres but if our people, even under the present legislation, are to be completely and properly served, especially in these more or less isolated districts, provision should be made for a larger number of advance polls.
Finally, I simply want to say that the people who are denied the right to vote under the present legislation are usually workers involved in our primary industries in isolated places who are helping to increase the production of this country, people who have the right to vote and who treasure their vote. We want all Canadians to vote and I do urge the minister to give serious consideration to amendments to the present act to remove this injustice suffered, I presume, by hundreds of thousands of Canadians under the present law.

subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: Order. I recognize the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond.

subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to say a few words on this matter and follow up what the hon. member for Kootenay West has said about advance polls. There are two features with respect to advance polls that should be given attention within a reasonable length of time. I do not know whether it is possible to do it between now and the next election. I hope it is. These matters should be given attention because not only do the conditions outlined by the hon. member for Kootenay West arise but in a constituency such as mine something else happens.
There are a large number of fishermen in my constituency.
They generally come home on Friday night and have to spend all day Saturday fixing up their nets and getting their boats in order to go out again on Sunday. The advance poll is generally set for the Friday and Saturday prior to election day. The result of that is that these men, because they are not included in the schedule of those permitted to vote at advance polls, are disfranchised.
Furthermore, under the present schedule of districts that are eligible for advance polls the returning officer is confined in a constituency such as mine to Burnaby. The Richmond area cannot have an advance poll. Now that is wrong in principle because the fishermen all reside in the Richmond area. They are disfranchised because the returning officer cannot set up a second advance poll in Richmond. Then again when the advance poll is set up in Burnaby these men have to travel about 12 to 14 miles if they want to go there.
I am not a bit surprised that under the present system of enumeration we get a great deal of skipped enumeration. When an enumerator is paid only ten cents a name and finds a person absent from home there is not the foggiest chance in the world of that enumerator going back again. I would not blame him. I would suggest to the minister that consideration be given to raising the amount paid enumerators. I would point out that the return of ten cents per name has been in effect since 1934. It has not been altered during all that time. I would suggest that the cost of enumeration today is not too high when one considers the work that is done. If we are going to insist on enumeration, then we should take every possible step we can to be sure that the enumerators are properly compensated so that they will carry out their work in an efficient manner. You cannot expect an enumerator to call at a home three or four times for the ten cents paid for securing one name. It cannot be done.
I would suggest that the minister take up the question of a running enumeration, that

is a voters list which is permanent, as we do in British Columbia. The voters lists are kept permanently and any person can get on the voters list whenever he wants. If a person moves from one place to another, he can get on the voters list there. The result is that the voters list is always up to date. I realize that would mean establishing a permanent registry of voters, such as we have in British Columbia, but that is less costly than enumeration.
I should like also to support the request of one of the other members for a reconsideration of the line rate that is paid for printing the voters list. This is not a question of unions or anything like that, but at the moment the line rate is such that printers cannot take voters lists in union shops. The line rate for printing these voters lists has not been changed for many years. It is about time that these matters were given a little consideration. I do not believe an amendment to the act would be required to take care of these things.
There is one other little matter which could be rectified by a change in the act. At the present time when the returning officer sets up polling areas one would naturally expect that he would put the polling station in the middle of the polling district. However, they do not do that. They set up a polling district and then they set the polling station over in one corner of it. The result is that in an area like Burnaby, what happened in two different places was that the polling station was established in such a way that people who were living within three quarters of a mile of the polling station had to travel nearly four miles to get to it, simply because it happened to be on the other side of a creek. I would suggest the returning officers be instructed to set polling stations where they will be equally accessible to all persons within a given polling area.
With regard to the matter of putting the political affiliation of a candidate on the ballot, I think that is a must. Now that there are quite a number of parties participating in an election I feel the people should know the affiliation of the person for whom they are voting. There are plenty of people who vote for the party. They do not know the candidates and do not know whether they are Liberals or Conservatives. I think they should be given a chance to vote for their party if they feel like it. There is no reason why they should not be given that opportunity. May I point out that the service vote is strictly on party lines because a serviceman can write in the name of the party on the ballot, not name the candidate at all, and that
Supply-Secretary of State vote will be accepted. If that procedure is valid for the service vote, why should it not be valid for the civilian vote?

subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
While I have never been noted particularly for my gallantry, I sincerely congratulate the minister upon her ascendancy to the high position she holds. I might say further that is probably one indication of the fact that the bill which she brought forward so assiduously concerning equal pay for equal work for women was not so important after all.
I join particularly in supporting the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond in his observations that we are not paying the printers sufficient for printing the voters lists. In my travels during the last campaign I visited the printing office of one of the weekly newspapers. I noted they were not busily engaged in printing the voters lists. I asked him why that was so. He said he could not afford to do it, his time was too valuable, and he could not afford to hire help. He had no interest in printing the voters lists.
I cannot agree with the hon. member for Timmins that there is a great deal of patronage with respect to this, because it seemed to me that almost all the newspaper offices I visited were busily engaged in that work. They all had the same complaint, that they were not being paid sufficiently for the work they were undertaking.

subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: How about the candidate paying for his own printing, ballots and everything. The hon. member said there was no patronage, so how about the member paying for everything.

subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
I have no knowledge of what might have happened in the hon. member's riding, but I know in my riding those things did not happen.
The question of paying enumerators is also one which I am sure would not require a revision of the act. I am sure that an order in council might very well provide for a higher rate for each name an enumerator put on the list. This pay is not sufficient even in the urban areas, but the greatest difficulty is encountered in ridings which are predominantly rural. I feel that something should be done before the next general election.
With respect to the grievance which the hon. member for Kootenay West had, namely that constituents may be away fighting fires, perhaps that matter is not so urgent. This may transpire before the real hot weather comes so I do not think this matter is as urgent as is the need of increased rates of pay to the printers and to the enumerators.

Supply-Secretary of State
With respect to changing the act in order to provide for enlarging the number of people who would be able to vote at advance polls,
I think that is something that needs to be studied by a committee and I have no further recommendations on that matter. I have heard that innumerable difficulties would crop up if that course were to be undertaken. At the present time I do not want to press that point. I think the main thing to be kept in mind is that an election is pending, and I think the rates for the printers and for the enumerators should be given thorough and early consideration.

subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
May I first offer my congratulations to the Secretary of State. I am not very often shocked, or at least that is what I am told, but when I went to the United Nations in September I was terrifically shocked to find that no government employee who is posted or who is on duty outside of Canada can vote. I see no reason why these people who are serving our country should not be in the same category as are the armed forces. The situation is very unfortunate. For example, at our embassy in New York, the clerks, the chauffeurs, the office help, and even the ambassador are not allowed to vote because the government has sent them there on duty and by so doing has disfranchised them and deprived them of their opportunity of voting. That is something that I shall discuss further.
What I wanted to say this afternoon is this and I have given this matter a great deal of thought. When the proper authorities come to discuss how this matter can be dealt with I shall offer some suggestions. I have worked out a system that I think will be all right. The first thing you must do is to preserve the secrecy of those that are voting. In some areas across this country there might be only two or three employees there and that matter would have to be guarded very carefully. I should be glad to offer my suggestions at the proper time when this matter is discussed.

subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
I should just like to ask a few questions of the minister. I should like to know how much money each individual returning officer in a constituency is permitted to spend in advertising two things, first, the courts of revision within the constituency and, second, the hours that employees may have off from work under the election act.
I make this further point in connection with the court of revision. To the junior chamber of commerce in our area which spends a great deal of time advertising the actual election day, I have suggested that they could take up this particular chore of advertising the court of revision.

I want to close with the comment that I hope the development in Toronto where they had the difficulty over the certificates that went to the court of revision will not lead to any change because we found those particular certificates to be very useful on the part of all parties at Port Arthur. The certificates to which I am referring are the ones where people go into committee rooms and fill out a petition and then the committee room people can take it over to the court of revision. We found that certificate to be extremely useful and I think it should be retained.

subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
May I also congratulate the Secretary of State on her appointment as minister for that department. I should like to back up the statements made by the hon. member for Fraser Valley with regard to names left off the voters' list. I say that because I had some experience with regard to it in the last election. Odd as it may seem, the enumerator came around to our own place and we were enumerated and given receipts. We had first, of course, looked at the main list nailed up on telephone poles and found that our names were not there. On the day of the election when we went down to vote ours were the only two names that appeared on the revised list.
I had about ten or so calls from people who were concerned about the fact that when they looked at the regular list which was posted they found that their names were not there. Then they went down on the day of revision to have their names put on the list. As far as I can understand it, the people in charge there took down the names on a book-that is on the poll book-and said, "Your name will appear on the voters' list." But when they went to vote their names were not on the voters' list. The fact that they had been enumerated and had slips did not give them the authority to vote. These people had absolutely no recourse whatever.
That sort of thing happened in the very poll at which I was myself. As I say, my wife's name and mine appeared on the list and we were the only two in the whole poll. The voter is put in a very bad position. He complies with the law. After enumeration is made he is given his slip, if he is in an urban area, showing that he has been enumerated. Then he checks the list when it appears in a public place, such as on a telephone pole or whatever it is. He finds that his name is not there. He goes down on the day of revision to have it put on. Then when he goes to vote on election day and finds that his name is not there, it is a serious matter. These people have complied with all the laws and all the regulations with regard to the matter and yet they are disfranchised.

To the minister and those in charge of this matter I suggest that there possibly is a way in which to overcome this difficulty. When the voter finds that his name is not on the regularly posted list it seems to me that when he goes on the day of revision to have his name put on the list he should at that time be given a card which has on it an appropriate government stamp to show that he has the right to vote, whether his name appears on the final revised list or not. He has gone to the trouble to inspect the list. He finds his name is not there. He goes down on the day of revision to have it put on the list. Yet when he comes to the poll, he finds that he is still not on it.
It seems to me that it would be a very simple thing for the government to send out cards which could not be duplicated, with government stamps on them, and which would be handed out by the returning officer on those days of revision so that such a person would be assured, after having gone to all this trouble, that he would have his vote when the day came. It would not be a very costly matter because there would not be many cards sent to each city. I would not imagine that there would be over 50, 75 or 100 in each case. It would be a simple process. It would assure the voter that he would at least have the right to vote after he has gone to all the trouble of making the proper inspection. I hope the minister will give this suggestion some consideration.

subtopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
I would like to concur in the remarks made by other hon. members with respect to advance polls. As the minister knows, although the act says that people working on transportation are allowed to vote at advance polls, this does not apply in the Northwest Territories. We have somewhat different conditions in the Northwest Territories from those in most other parts of
Supply-Secretary of State Canada, not only in respect to transportation. We have people working on water transportation, aviation, fishing, trapping and the like and, with no advance polls at which to register their votes, what happens? Frequently- as a matter of fact at just about every election-these people in varying walks of life are disenfranchised. I think the house should try to make it possible for as many of our citizens to exercise their right to vote as possible.
Now, as I have said, in the north these trappers and fishermen, because of their occupation, find it necessary to travel from one point to another. For instance in the last election we had people normally resident in Fort Providence and Fort Simpson who, because there was not sufficient work available for them, had to move, say, to Great Slave lake to fish for their livelihood. These people normally appear on the voters' lists in the posts or towns in which they reside. I think the situation in the Yukon is also different; people are nomadic and move from point to point in order to make their living; they had to go say from Whitehorse to Carmacks or to the United Keno mine, or some other part of the Yukon in order to make their living and so were disenfranchised. When they went to the polling booth the returning officer or his deputy would know that they were residents of long standing in the Yukon in the majority of cases and he would allow them to vote. He knew they passed the residence qualifications but, when the matter came before the courts, approximately 500 votes of a total of 5,000 registered in the Yukon were thrown out. In other words 10 per cent of those people who did cast their votes-there were many others who did not-by the actions of the courts in charge in the Yukon were disenfranchised.
Now I think hon. members will agree that 10 per cent of the people who actually vote is a very high proportion of the total figure in any constituency. I would like to suggest to the minister that with respect to the Yukon and the Northwest Territories special provision should be made.
